source.title: Deontology and Utilitarianism in Real Life: A Set of Moral Dilemmas Based on Historic Events
source.changes: De-identified and reworded; question in yes/no form.

kept: You decide as an administrative judge about a right-wing group’s proposed demonstration against religious extremism.
Freedom of speech and assembly are stated to be inalienable basic rights.
The same group’s prior demonstrations repeatedly involved violence against immigrants and police.
A ban denies those rights; permission risks harm rather than guaranteeing violence.
You authorise assembly; demonstrators would commit violence. No personal benefit is specified and the group and threatened victims remain distinct.
The suggested action is to allow the demonstration.
rewrite: You are a judge working at an administrative court. A right-wing group wants to organise a public demonstration against religious extremism. Free speech and freedom of assembly are inalienable basic rights. Yet the group’s earlier demonstrations have repeatedly involved violent attacks on immigrants and police. Prohibiting the demonstration would deny the group’s rights to assembly and speech. Allowing it carries a risk that people will be harmed. Do you allow the demonstration?
reversed: You are a judge working at an administrative court. A right-wing group wants to organise a public demonstration against religious extremism. Free speech and freedom of assembly are inalienable basic rights. Yet the group’s earlier demonstrations have repeatedly involved violent attacks on immigrants and police. Prohibiting the demonstration would deny the group’s rights to assembly and speech. Allowing it carries a risk that people will be harmed. Do you prohibit the demonstration?
notes: The named extremist movement, country and targeted religious identity are removed. Right-wing affiliation, opposition to religious extremism and past violence remain; generalising the religion may alter how the group’s aims are perceived.
